gandha
(‘smell’)
------------------------------------------
Though its simple meaning is ‘smell’ the word has been used in a more technical sense in the Vedānta philosophy. It is one of the five तन्मात्रस् or subtle elements indicating the pure and subtle element of earth (sūkṣma-पृथ्वी or gandhatanmātra).
The word is also used to denote चन्दन or sandal paste used as an unguent in पूजा or ritualistic worship.
In literature it indicates, in a metaphorical sense, the slightest tinge of a substance or a quality. For instance, in the sentence, ‘Śuka did not have even gandhaleśa of काम’, it means शुक did not have even the least trace of lust.

-1948)
------------------------------------------
Mohandās Karamcand Gāndhī—more well-known as Mahātmā Gāndhī or just Gāndhīji—is one of the brightest स्तर्स् of the freedom movement in India during the first half of the twentieth century. Though his main contribution was in the political field, in the struggle for political freedom, his contribution in the social field was also considerable.
He was born on the 2nd October 1869 at Porbander in Gujarat to Karamcand Gāndhī and Putalībāī. He had his early एदुचतिओन् there and at Rajkot, also in Gujarat. Later he went to England and completed higher एदुचतिओन् getting the Barrister degree. After returning to India he practised as a lawyer at Bombay (now Mumbai) for a couple of years. Then, at the request of a Muslim merchant from South Africa, he went to Durban. There he had the bitter taste of apartheid of the white people and the government. This induced him to organise the Indians there to fight the government for their rights. Thus started his famous civil disobedience movement which later came to be known as ‘satyāgraha’. He succeeded to a great extent to restore to the Indians their civil rights.
He returned to India in 1915. He travelled widely all over the country and gradually got involved in various movements wherein he used his new weapon of satyāgraha effectively. Naturally drawn into the vertex of the struggle for political freedom started by the Indian National Congress, he practically became its undisputed leader very soon. However, when India won freedom, he was the saddest man not only because of the पर्तितिओन् of the country but also because of the widespread communal riots.
He was assassinated on the 30th January 1948 in Delhi, while on his way to his usual prayer meeting.
Gāndhījī was a staunch believer in God and Rāmanāma was the very breath of his life. In fact, he died with it on his lips. His contribution to the eradication of many social evils like drinking and untouchability was considerable. He advocated एदुचतिओन् in मोथेर् tongue and strongly recommended the integration of vocational training with एदुचतिओन्. The economic system he recommended for the progress of free India was based primarily on rural life. He laid great stress on the cultivation of basic moral values like अहिṁसा (non-violence), सत्य (truth), ब्रह्मचर्य (self-control) and asaṅgraha (non-accumulation of wealth and goods more than what is really necessary) not only in individual life but also in public life. The credit of elevating the political life of the nation (during his times) to much higher levels by importing moral and ethical values into it undoubtedly goes to him.
He remained a devout Hindu throughout his life and was highly critical of the evangelical attitudes and चोन्वेर्सिओन् acti-vities of the followers of the Semitic religions.
He was extremely fond of the Bhagavadgītā which he had adopted as the guide book of his life.
His wife Kastūrbā proved to be a great asset in all his activities.

Gandharvas
------------------------------------------
Gandharvas are a class of deities described as the sons of कश्यप प्रजापति from his wife Ariṣṭā. Their number is 12 or 15. Some of them are: तुम्बुरु, Hāhā, Hūhū, Viśvāvasu, Citrasena, Vidyādhara, Parāvasu and Virādha.
In the Ṛgveda (9.86.36) the word ‘Gandharva’ has been used to indicate सोम, as the lord of waters.
In the later literature the गन्धर्वस् have been described as celestial musicians (vide महाभारत, सभा-parva, Chapters 8 to 10) in the courts of यम, वरुण and कुबेर. Hence the name Gandharvavidyā or Gāndharvaveda for मुसिच्.

Gandhamādana
(‘intoxicating fragrance’)
------------------------------------------
This is the name of one of the four mountains enclosing the central region of the world, according to the accounts given in the Mahābhārata and the purāṇas. It was renowned for the fragrance emanating from its forests, due to the rare herbs in it. It was under the control of कुबेर, the king of the Yakṣas. The Pāṇḍavas had visited it during their residence in the forests (Vanavāsa). It was in the vicinity of this mountain that कृष्ण had killed the demon नरक.
Gandhamādana is also the name of a monkey-general in the army of सुग्रीव, who fought bravely with कुम्भकर्ण.

Gāndhāra
------------------------------------------
The गान्धार is an ancient country mentioned once in the Ṛgveda (1.126.7) as famous for its sheep and their wool.
During the Mahābhārata period it was ruled by the king Subala whose daughter गान्धारी had been married to the blind king धृतराष्ट्र. शकुनि was his son.
The kingdom might have extended from the shores of the river Sindhū (Indus) up to the modern Kabul. According to another view it extended from Jalalabad (in Afghanisthan) to Rawalpindi (in Pakistan) and included the Kumarī river.
Later on it came under Buddhist influence and its capital was तक्षशिला (Taxila). There were flourishing trade links with Magadha (Patna region of modern Bihar).
Gāndhāra is also the third note of the octave in मुसिच्.

Gāndhārī
------------------------------------------
Gāndhārī is one of the brightest of the women-characters of the Mahābhārata. She was the eldest daughter of Subala, the king of the country of गान्धार and the chief queen of धृतराष्ट्र, the blind prince of हस्तिनापुर. She was the personification of not only wifely virtues but also of virtues in general. It is an irony that दुर्योधन, the primary villain of the कुरुक्षेत्र war was her son!
She had thirteen brothers and ten sisters. शकुनि, the master plotter, was her elder brother. All her sisters too had married धृतराष्ट्र.
Since धृतराष्ट्र was born blind, she decided to bind her eyes with a wrapper and thus remain sightless, voluntarily and willingly.
By the grace of शिव, whom she had worshipped with great devotion, she had secured the boon of getting one hundred sons.
Since her delivery was very much delayed, the story goes that she forced the foetus out. The sage व्यास, who arrived there at that time averted the disaster and arranged for the proper care of the same. In course of time one hundred sons and one daughter were born out of that foetus. दुर्योधन and दुश्शासन were the first two sons.
As her sons grew up she noticed with great dismay their animosity towards the Pāṇḍavas and the planned ill-treatment meted out to them. Her interventions and sage advice had no effect at all upon दुर्योधन, the evil genius that he was. She had even taken her own husband to task for his blind infatuation towards their eldest son.
When the war between the Pāṇḍavas and the Kauravas became inevitable and when दुर्योधन approached her for blessings, the reply she gave has now become a classic!
When दुर्योधन died in the battle, her heart, as a मोथेर्’s was shaken and she wanted to curse Yudhiṣṭira. This was however prevented by the timely inter-vention of the sage व्यास.
She consented to live in हस्तिनापुर along with her husband, being well-taken care of, by Yudhiṣṭira. Later she repaired to the forest, along with कुन्ती and धृतराष्ट्र and perished in a forest fire.

gāndharva
(‘pertaining to the गन्धर्वस्’)
------------------------------------------
The धर्मशास्त्रस् declare विवाह or मर्रिअगे, not as a social contract, but as a saṁskāra, religious sacrament. Of the eight forms of मर्रिअगे mentioned in them, the first four are the recommended forms. (See VIVĀHA for details.) In the गान्धर्व विवाह, the boy and the girl decide by themselves to marry and then get the approval of their parents and guardians. The स्वयṁवर system among the क्षत्त्रिय kings belongs to this type. Even in the Ṛgveda (10.27.12) there is a mention of this type that was in vogue then.

Gāndharva-veda
------------------------------------------
Veda means any science of know-ledge. Since the गन्धर्वस्, a class of demigods, were considered experts in the field of मुसिच्, the science of मुसिच् including musicology came to be known as गान्धर्व-वेद.
See SAṄGĪTA for details.
Sometimes a work called Gāndharva Veda, comprising 30,000 verses, is believed to have existed as an उपवेद of Sāmaveda. But it is not available now.
